activities.anchor: Every word can be parsed this way
activities.caption: assemble the word, layer by layer
activities.name: morParseOrder

config.prompt: The parse forms a tree — assemble unbelievably in attachment order:
items: un- attaches to the whole of believable → unbelievable
config.why: The layering is not negotiable — *believe-un-ly-able is impossible — and it is the same hierarchical thinking the syntax lesson applies to sentences.

activities.anchor: Not every bound morpheme is a neat prefix or suffix
activities.caption: pair the exotic morpheme with its machinery
activities.name: morWeaveMatch

config.prompt: Beyond prefixes and suffixes — pair the form with its machinery:

pairs.right: English's only productive infix — placed right before the stressed syllable
root-and-pattern: the consonantal root k-t-b interleaved with vowel patterns
a cranberry morpheme — a meaning contribution that occurs nowhere else

config.why: Meaning built by weaving, not gluing — and some morphemes are orphans: morphology's fossils.

activities.caption: file each affixation by the job it does
activities.name: morAffixBuckets

config.prompt: Two jobs, two boxes — file each:
buckets: derivation — new word, new dictionary entry
config.why: Inflected forms fill grammar tables (the lexeme is listed once); derivational families fill dictionaries with new entries — and derivational affixes sit closer to the root: teach-er-s, never teach-s-er.

activities.caption: count the endings — English versus Latin
activities.name: morEndingsEstimate

config.prompt: How many productive inflectional endings does modern English run?
config.why: About six — plural -s, past -ed, -ing, comparative -er, genitive 's, third-person -s — where Latin or Finnish run to dozens per noun or verb. The thinness is historical erosion, and it explains English's hard reliance on word order and imported derivational parts (bio-, -ology, -ify).
config.context: Old English was much more inflected — the endings wore away, the work moved.

activities.anchor: languages sort along a spectrum of morphemes-per-word
activities.caption: drag the divider — particles versus one-word clauses
activities.name: morSpecCompare

config.prompt: The packaging spectrum's two poles — drag the divider:

before.label: Analytic — Mandarin
before.text: Roughly one morpheme per word; grammatical work done by separate particles and word order.

after.label: Polysynthetic — Inuktitut, Mohawk
after.text: Entire clauses in one word: the verb can include its subject, object, direction and location.

config.why: Between them: agglutinative (Turkish, Finnish, Swahili — one meaning per piece) and fusional (Latin, Russian — several meanings in one unbreakable ending). Packaging, not complexity: Mandarin is not 'simpler' than Inuktitut.

activities.anchor: Derivation is only one machine in the word factory
activities.caption: pair each coinage with the machine that built it
activities.name: morFactoryMatch

config.prompt: The word factory's production lines — pair the words with their process:

pairs.left: burgle (from burglar), edit (from editor), babysit (from babysitter)
pairs.right: backformation — reverses history, subtracting an imagined affix

pairs.left: a google, to friend, an ask
pairs.right: conversion — changes class without changing form

config.why: Compounding (snowmageddon, bookshop, pickpocket) is the other big line — each process has favourite territories, and a word's formation tells you its age and social origin.

activities.anchor: But machines are not equally busy
activities.caption: find the line the dead affix forbids
activities.name: morProductSpot

config.prompt: One line of this productivity report is wrong — click it:
lines: -ness and -able attach to almost anything new — binge-watchability works.
-th is dead, surviving only in frozen relics: warmth, depth, width.
An affix's share of recent coinages, scored against its share of the whole lexicon, measures its output.
You can coin *coolth and it passes as ordinary English.
The affixes people will apply to nonsense words are the productive ones — the wug-test logic.
config.correction: *coolth needs a wink — speakers who use it know it is a joke.
config.why: Frozen relics stay frozen; the measurable test is recent coinages, which is the direct ancestor of the wug-test logic.

activities.anchor: The inflectional side of morphology does the grammar's bookkeeping
activities.caption: drop the marker on Finnish's case count
activities.name: morCasePlace

config.prompt: Latin runs six cases, German four, Russian six. How many does Finnish run?
config.why: Fifteen — the endings carry each noun's role regardless of order (puella canem amat and canem puella amat mean the same). English lost almost all of it — genitive 's and pronouns (I/me, he/him) survive — and paid with rigid word order. Agreement is the other currency: 'she walks', French adjective gender, Swahili's noun-class concord.
